questions.q: How far from Earth is the L1 point, where Aditya-L1 works?
questions.do: Read the Where they are table, row L1.
questions.a: About 1,497,621 km, roughly 1.5 million km towards the Sun. That matches ISRO’s “about 1.5 million km”.

questions.q: Which loop height gives a halo orbit that takes exactly as long as Aditya-L1’s real one?
questions.do: In Aditya-L1’s halo orbit, move the slider How far the loop rises above Earth’s orbit plane step by step and watch Time for one lap.
questions.a: About 120,000 km out of the plane gives 177.86 days, ISRO’s figure for Aditya-L1. The whole family only ranges from about 177.59 to 177.89 days, so the lap time hardly changes with size.

questions.q: Let a spacecraft go near L1, then near L4. Which point holds on to it?
questions.do: In Give it a nudge, click L1 (Aditya-L1, SOHO) and read the results. Then click L4 (Trojan asteroids at Jupiter) and compare.
questions.a: From just 300 km off L1, it is more than 1 million km away after about 190 days: it slides off. From 100,000 km off L4 it wanders up to about 81 million km but never escapes, looping back about every 230 years.

questions.q: Why does Aditya-L1 have to fire its thrusters a few times every year?
questions.do: Click L1 (Aditya-L1, SOHO) in Give it a nudge and read the message. Then read the row Why station-keeping is needed in the checks table.
questions.a: L1 is like the top of a saddle. A small error grows by about 2.7 times every 23 days, about 8 million times in a year if left alone. Small, regular burns (0.2 to 4 m/s a year) keep it on its halo orbit.

questions.q: Who found the five balance points, and when? Who later worked out halo orbits?
questions.do: Read the introduction at the top of the page and the Method line in the footer.
questions.a: Joseph-Louis Lagrange, in 1772. Halo orbits came much later, from R. W. Farquhar (1968) and K. C. Howell (1984). Aditya-L1 launched on 2 September 2023 and arrived on 6 January 2024.
